`axolotl export` converts a trained checkpoint into [GGUF](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md), the format used by llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, and llamafile.

::: {.callout-note}

GGUF is for the llama.cpp family of runtimes. For **vLLM, SGLang, or TGI**, serve the merged safetensors checkpoint directly (see [merge-lora](./cli.qmd#merge-lora)), optionally quantized with [torchao](./quantize.qmd) or llm-compressor — vLLM's GGUF loader is experimental and slower than its native path.

:::

## Prerequisites

Export shells out to a built [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) checkout, which is not a Python dependency of Axolotl:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
export LLAMA_CPP_DIR=$PWD/llama.cpp
cmake -S $LLAMA_CPP_DIR -B $LLAMA_CPP_DIR/build && cmake --build $LLAMA_CPP_DIR/build --config Release -j
```

Point at it with `$LLAMA_CPP_DIR` or the `export.llama_cpp_dir` config key. Building is only required if you request quantized outputs; `llama-quantize` is looked up in `$LLAMA_CPP_DIR/build/bin/`, `$LLAMA_CPP_DIR/`, then `$PATH`.

::: {.callout-warning}

Do not `pip install -r llama.cpp/requirements/...` into your training environment. Those files pin an older `transformers` and a CPU-only `torch`, which would replace the versions Axolotl depends on. The conversion script runs under Axolotl's interpreter, which already has everything it needs, and it loads `gguf-py` from the checkout itself.

:::

## Usage

```bash
axolotl export config.yml --quantize Q4_K_M,Q8_0
```

## LoRA adapters

Set `export.lora` and an unmerged LoRA/QLoRA run exports as a *standalone GGUF LoRA* instead, through llama.cpp's [`convert_lora_to_gguf.py`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/convert_lora_to_gguf.py). The adapter is not a model on its own. It is loaded at runtime on top of a GGUF of the same base model, so both files have to be present:

```bash
axolotl export config.yml --lora
llama-cli -m base-f16.gguf --lora outputs/my-run/gguf/my-run-lora-f32.gguf
```

```yaml
export:
  lora: true
```

Without it, an adapter-only `output_dir` is refused and points you at `axolotl merge-lora`. Training pre-saves the base model's `config.json` beside the adapter, so the converter reads the base config locally instead of fetching it from the Hub.

Two options work differently here. `quantize` is rejected, because `llama-quantize` only takes full models, and `outtype` is limited to `f32`, `f16`, `bf16`, `q8_0`, `auto`. It defaults to `f32` rather than `f16`, matching `convert_lora_to_gguf.py`'s own default. The default filename gains a `-lora` marker (`{output_dir}/gguf/{run}-lora-{ftype}.gguf`) so an adapter export cannot overwrite a full-model one.

## Configuration

Options are named after their `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` counterparts:

```yaml
export:
  format: gguf         # Optional[str] = "gguf". Deployment format.
  outtype: f16         # Optional[str]. Weight type of the conversion: f32, f16, bf16, q8_0, tq1_0, tq2_0, auto. Defaults to f16, or f32 for a LoRA export.
  quantize: [Q4_K_M]   # Optional[list[str]] = []. Additional llama.cpp quant types to emit.
  outfile:             # Optional[str]. Defaults to {output_dir}/gguf/{run}-{ftype}.gguf.
  llama_cpp_dir:       # Optional[str]. Defaults to $LLAMA_CPP_DIR.
  lora: false          # Optional[bool] = false. Export the adapter as a standalone GGUF LoRA instead of a full model.
```

Every key can be overridden from the CLI (`--outtype`, `--quantize`, `--outfile`, `--llama-cpp-dir`, `--lora/--no-lora`), and `--model-dir` exports an arbitrary checkpoint instead of the one in `output_dir`.

As in llama.cpp, `{ftype}` in `outfile` is replaced by the weight type, so each requested quant type is written as its own file alongside the unquantized conversion:

```
outputs/my-run/gguf/
├── my-run-f16.gguf
├── my-run-Q4_K_M.gguf
└── my-run-Q8_0.gguf
```

## Preflight checks

Conversion is slow, so a few failure modes are caught up front:

- **Pre-quantized checkpoints** (torchao fp8/nvfp4, bitsandbytes) cannot be converted — re-export in bf16 with `axolotl merge-lora --dequant`.
- **Vocab mismatch** between `tokenizer.json` and `config.json` (a common outcome of adding tokens without resizing embeddings).
- **Multi-token-prediction layers** (`num_nextn_predict_layers`), which llama.cpp cannot load. See the [GLM-4.5 example](https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl/tree/main/examples/glm45).
- **Missing chat template**, which is only a warning but usually means the runtime will fall back to a default template and undo your fine-tune.

A LoRA export runs its own checks instead, for the two things the adapter converter cannot represent:

- **DoRA** (`peft_use_dora`). The converter only pairs up `lora_A`/`lora_B` tensors and has no handling for DoRA's magnitude vectors.
- **`lora_modules_to_save`**, whose layers PEFT writes out whole rather than as a low-rank pair.

In both cases the fix is the same, which is to merge the adapter with `axolotl merge-lora` and export the merged model.

## Known gaps

Not yet supported: importance-matrix (`imatrix`) calibration, `gguf-split` for large models, multimodal `mmproj` files, and pushing to the Hub.
